title: 1 Samuel 1:9–18
context: At Shiloh, Hannah pours out her soul to the LORD and vows to give him a son. Eli the priest first mistakes her for a drunk woman, then blesses her, and she goes away no longer sad.

verses.text: So Hannah rose up after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh. Now Eli the priest was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of the LORD’s temple.
verses.arminianNotes: After the meal Hannah rises, while Eli sits by the doorpost of the LORD’s temple. Arminian readers see Hannah taking the initiative to seek God herself rather than remaining passive in her grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hannah moving from the family table to the place of prayer. Eli’s seated posture at the doorway introduces the aging priest who will misread her before he blesses her.

verses.text: She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed to the LORD, weeping bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes: In bitterness of soul Hannah prays to the LORD, weeping bitterly. Arminian readers see honest lament welcomed by God, who invites his people to bring their anguish to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see bitter prayer as faith directed to God rather than away from him. The verse models a prayer that does not hide pain but carries it into God’s presence.

verses.text: She vowed a vow, and said, “LORD of Armies, if you will indeed look at the affliction of your servant and remember me, and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a boy, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah vows, “LORD of Armies, if you will indeed look at the affliction of your servant … then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life.” Arminian readers see a sincere vow freely offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a devoted vow that returns the hoped-for gift to God. The promise that “no razor shall come on his head” recalls Nazirite language in Numbers 6:5 and Judges 13:5.

verses.text: As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli saw her mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: As Hannah keeps praying, Eli watches her mouth. Arminian readers see persistence in prayer, as Hannah continues before the LORD even while she is being observed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hannah’s continued prayer before the LORD. Eli watches outward movements without yet knowing the heart, a point that matters in the misunderstanding that follows.

verses.text: Now Hannah spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk.
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah speaks in her heart; only her lips move, so Eli thinks she is drunk. Arminian readers see inward, heartfelt prayer that a religious leader fails to recognize.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priest misjudging sincere devotion. The scene quietly anticipates the larger failure of discernment in Eli’s house that the following chapters expose.

verses.text: Eli said to her, “How long will you be drunk? Get rid of your wine!”
verses.arminianNotes: Eli says, “How long will you be drunk? Get rid of your wine!” Arminian readers see a harsh rebuke that wounds an already grieving woman who had come to pray.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Eli’s hasty judgment. The irony is that Eli rebukes Hannah for imagined excess while failing to restrain his sons’ real abuses at the sanctuary.

verses.text: Hannah answered, “No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit. I have not been drinking wine or strong drink, but I poured out my soul before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah answers, “No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit … I poured out my soul before the LORD.” Arminian readers see a humble, truthful reply that corrects the priest respectfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hannah describing true prayer as pouring out the soul before God. Her answer is both courteous and honest, a model of speaking truth to those in authority.

verses.text: Don’t consider your servant a wicked woman; for I have been speaking out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation.”
verses.arminianNotes: She asks Eli not to consider her “a wicked woman,” explaining she has spoken from her complaint and provocation. Arminian readers see Hannah defending her integrity while owning her distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see lament distinguished from wickedness. Hannah’s words show that bringing complaint and provocation to God is not sinful but an expression of dependence on him.

verses.text: Then Eli answered, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Eli answers, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.” Arminian readers see the priest moving from rebuke to blessing once he hears the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Eli’s blessing as a priestly word of peace. The language of asking and petition prepares for the wordplay in Samuel’s naming and Hannah’s later testimony.

verses.text: She said, “Let your servant find favor in your sight.” So the woman went her way and ate; and her facial expression wasn’t sad any more.
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah says, “Let your servant find favor in your sight,” then eats, and her face is no longer sad. Arminian readers see faith resting in God before the answer is visible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see peace given before the promise is fulfilled. Hannah’s changed countenance shows trust that leaves her petition with God, though nothing outward has yet changed.
